title: Directions on the Road
summary: We practised asking for and giving directions in the street and on the road. We learned how to make question tags and how to say them with rising or falling intonation. We also learned polite indirect questions like 'Can you tell me where the bank is?'

grammar.title: Question tags
grammar.explain: A question tag is a short question at the end of a sentence, like 'aren't you?'. We use it to check information or to ask someone to agree with us. A positive sentence usually has a negative tag, and a negative sentence has a positive tag.
grammar.explain_ar: سؤال الذيل (question tag) هو سؤال قصير في نهاية الجملة مثل aren't you?. نستخدمه للتأكد من معلومة أو لنطلب من الشخص أن يوافقنا. الجملة المثبتة يأتي بعدها ذيل منفي، والجملة المنفية يأتي بعدها ذيل مثبت.
form: Positive sentence + negative tag: You're still coming, aren't you?
Negative sentence + positive tag: You haven't ordered yet, have you?
Use the same auxiliary or modal verb (be, have, can, will...) + pronoun.
No auxiliary? Use do / does / did: It starts at 6 o'clock, doesn't it?
Special cases: I'm late, aren't I? / Get me a drink, would you? / Let's go, shall we?

examples.en: You haven't ordered food yet, have you?
You can get your own, can't you?
It starts at 6 o'clock, doesn't it?
examples.note: present simple with no auxiliary → does

examples.en: You have met Anna, haven't you?
It's not far from the station, is it?

mistakes.wrong: It starts at 6 o'clock, isn't it?
mistakes.right: It starts at 6 o'clock, doesn't it?
mistakes.why: 'starts' is present simple, so the tag uses does.
Use a pronoun in the tag, not the name.

mistakes.wrong: You haven't ordered yet, haven't you?
mistakes.right: You haven't ordered yet, have you?

mistakes.why: The tag for 'I am' is 'aren't I'.

quiz.why: Positive sentence with 'is' → negative tag 'isn't it'.

quiz.q: It's not far from the station, ___?

quiz.why: Present simple with no auxiliary → doesn't.
Modal 'can' in a positive sentence → can't.

grammar.title: Intonation in question tags
grammar.explain: The voice can go up or down on a question tag. If your voice goes up (rising ↗), you are not sure and you are really asking. If your voice goes down (falling ↘), you are quite sure and only want the other person to agree.
grammar.explain_ar: يمكن أن يرتفع الصوت أو ينخفض في سؤال الذيل. إذا ارتفع الصوت (↗) فأنت غير متأكد وتسأل سؤالاً حقيقياً. وإذا انخفض الصوت (↘) فأنت متأكد تقريباً وتريد فقط أن يوافقك الشخص الآخر.
form: Rising ↗ = checking, not sure: You haven't ordered yet, have you? ↗
Falling ↘ = confirming, quite sure: You haven't ordered yet, have you? ↘
Wh- questions usually fall: Where are you? ↘
Yes/No questions usually rise: Can you see The Body Shop on the corner? ↗

examples.note: The speaker is quite sure you are coming.

examples.en: You haven't ordered food yet, have you? ↗
Can you see The Body Shop on the corner? ↗

mistakes.wrong: Using rising intonation when you are already sure.
mistakes.right: Use falling intonation to confirm something you already know.
mistakes.why: Rising sounds like you are unsure and need a real answer.

quiz.q: You are not sure if your friend is coming. 'You're coming, aren't you?' Your voice should go…
quiz.why: Rising intonation = a real question, you are not sure.

quiz.q: You know the film starts at 8. 'It starts at 8, doesn't it?' Your voice should go…
'How do I get there from here?' usually has…
quiz.why: It is a wh- question (how), so it usually falls.

quiz.q: 'Can you see The Body Shop on the corner?' usually has…

grammar.title: Indirect questions (Can you tell me where…?)
grammar.explain: To ask for directions politely, we often start with 'Can you tell me…?' or 'Do you know…?'. After these phrases, the second part is like a normal sentence: subject + verb, with no question word order and no do/does/did.
grammar.explain_ar: لكي نسأل عن الطريق بأدب نبدأ غالباً بـ Can you tell me…? أو Do you know…?. بعد هذه العبارات يكون الجزء الثاني مثل جملة عادية: فاعل + فعل، بدون ترتيب السؤال وبدون do/does/did، لأن الجملة فيها سؤال واحد فقط.
form: Can you tell me / Could you tell me / Do you know + wh-word + subject + verb?
Where is the bank? → Can you tell me where the bank is?
Yes/No questions: Do you know + if / whether + subject + verb?
How do I get there? → Could you tell me how I get there?

examples.en: Can you tell me where the bank is?
Do you know which exit it is?
Could you tell me how I get to the station?
Do you know if the restaurant is far from here?

mistakes.wrong: Can you tell me where is the bank?
mistakes.right: Can you tell me where the bank is?
mistakes.why: After 'Can you tell me', use subject + verb (the bank is).

mistakes.wrong: Do you know where does Sarah live?
mistakes.right: Do you know where Sarah lives?
mistakes.why: No do/does in the second part.

mistakes.wrong: Do you know is the café open?
mistakes.right: Do you know if the café is open?

quiz.why: Subject + verb after the question word.

quiz.q: Could you tell me ___ the restaurant is open now?

options: Do you know how I get to the bank?
Do you know how do I get to the bank?
Do you know how get I to the bank?

quiz.q: Excuse me, can you tell me which exit ___?
quiz.why: Normal word order in the second part: it is.

phrases.en: How do I get there from here?
Can you tell me where the bank is?
Can you see The Body Shop on the corner?
Go out of the station and cross to the other side.
Go past The Body Shop and turn right.
Go around the roundabout and take the second exit.
